name: Life
miniText: How can a fixed local rule generate persistent structures and apparently purposeful motion? NetLogo Life implements Conway's binary cellular automaton: a dead cell is born with three living neighbors, while a living cell survives with two or three. Neighbor counts are computed before any cell changes, preserving synchronous generations on the model's wrapping square lattice. Gardner's original exposition [1] supplies the historical rule context; Wolfram [2] places such local deterministic systems within statistical studies of cellular automata; Adamatzky's edited research volume [3] develops their computational and organizational implications. Random initial density and manually drawn patterns expose extinction, oscillation, and moving configurations. The finite torus, discrete time, and deliberately abstract states are essential assumptions. These patterns illustrate rule-driven emergence and sensitivity to initial conditions, rather than biological population dynamics or empirical validation.
